# Office Deck (new presentation)

Builds a new PowerPoint deck with GenOffice's staged pipeline: you write design and content as files, and the `genoffice` engine checks each stage before the next one starts. Every presentation, however short, goes through this pipeline; ops are not hand-placed for a new deck.

## Behavior

The full version is `<package_root>/scripts/genoffice/SKILL.source.md`. It wins where this body differs, except for the changes listed in the Sources section. Open only the section a step points to.

1. **Check the engine.** Run `genoffice --version` first. If the command is not found, read the one line in `~/.genoffice/launcher` (Windows: `%USERPROFILE%\.genoffice\launcher`), which GenOffice writes on every start, and run `"<dir>/genoffice"` from bash or `"<dir>\genoffice.cmd"` from PowerShell / cmd, quoted, in place of `genoffice`; the default locations when that file is missing are in the original's opening paragraph. If GenOffice is not installed, install it: say in one line what is installed and from where (the release for this platform from https://github.com/genspark-ai/genoffice/releases), run it, then confirm with `genoffice --version`. If the installer needs the user or fails, say which step is theirs and stop this delivery; do not simulate a deck or build it another way. Always add `--json` when a program reads the output; read `status`, `error`, `suggestion` and `detail`, never parse `message`.
2. **Load the references.** Run `genoffice guide slides design` once per session, then `genoffice guide slides spec`. Take spec and op fields from the guide, never by guessing: it is generated from the validator and always current. Run `genoffice capabilities --json` once: use search, image search and image generation for facts and photos only when it says they are configured, and plan photo-free pages otherwise.
3. **Read the user's material.** You read it, not genoffice: md, txt, csv, pdf and images directly. Office files go through the CLI first; when the material is a docx, xlsx or pptx, or a PDF you cannot open yourself, open "Reading the user's files" in the original for the command and its limits. Take figures and wording from that material; never `cat` or `unzip` an Office file.
4. **Style and outline.** Make a folder for the deck. Write `deck/style.md` (colors, fonts, layout variants, one sentence of style), then `deck/outline.json` (core hook plus one entry per page: title, type, layout, brief with real figures, image_queries). Run `genoffice slides check deck/outline.json --json` and fix every error before going on. Show the outline to the user only if they asked to review it.
5. **One page per step.** Re-read `deck/style.md` and the page's outline entry, resolve its photos, write `deck/pages/NN.json` (one page object echoing the entry's `title`, `type`, `layout`) and run `genoffice slides check deck/pages/NN.json --json`; it finds `outline.json` and `style.md` one folder up and checks the page against entry N and the palette. Fix until `detail.audit`, `detail.outline.findings` and `detail.style.offPalette` are empty (a disagreement with the outline exits 1), then go to the next page. Never write several pages in one file or one step.
6. **Build.** `genoffice create --type pptx --spec deck/pages --outline deck/outline.json --out deck/deck.pptx --json`. It refuses to run while an outline page has no file or a page disagrees with its entry.
7. **Look and audit.** `genoffice slides render deck/deck.pptx --out deck/shots --json` and look at the PNGs; `genoffice slides audit deck/deck.pptx --json` for the geometry findings. Fix a page in its file, then `genoffice slides replace deck/deck.pptx --slide n --spec deck/pages/NN.json --json`. At most two fix rounds. Before reporting: `slides audit deck.pptx --json` has empty `detail.issues` (apply the `suggest` ops otherwise), and you ran `render deck.pptx --out shots --grid --json` and opened the contact sheet. Report the `.pptx` path and anything you left as is.

## Output handoff

Return `deck_outline` (outline path and page count), `deck_file` (the .pptx path) and `deck_review` (audit result, rendered shots, anything left as is) as JSON strings. For a mapped step, submit them through the coordinator's `record` command with the step's `map_id` and `capability`. Do not edit `<state_dir>/map.md` or `<state_dir>/state.json`; the coordinator is their only writer.

## Specifics

- Deck specs are px on a 1280×720 canvas, ops are EMU: never mix the two in one file.
- `--slide n` of `slides read/audit/render/replace` and op targets `{ "slide": n }` are 0-based; `render --page n` is 1-based. `s_0` is page 1 of the PNGs.
- Photos come from `genoffice search --images` results, `genoffice image` or local files the user gave you; never draw a grey box in place of a photo. Figures come from the user's material or `genoffice search`; say so when a number is illustrative.
- **Data leaving the machine:** every command runs headless on the app's own engines; only `search`, `image` and `media` send data off the machine (the query or the referenced file), to the provider configured in GenOffice.
- `create`, `convert` and `image` never overwrite (exit 2, `output_exists`): pick another name, or `--force` when the user asked for replacement. If `GENOFFICE_ALLOWED_ROOTS` is set, genoffice reads and writes only inside those directories (exit 2 otherwise); stay within them.
- Do not run `genoffice open` unless the user asks to see the file in GenOffice.
- When a command returns `status: "error"`: branch on `error`, do what `suggestion` says, then resend the whole batch. Open the table in "When a command fails" for the next command of that `error` value. `check` and `audit` exit 0 whether or not they found something. A successful result may still carry `warnings[]`: read them, report what matters, do not retry.

## Checks

- **outline_and_pages_checked**: `slides check` reported no errors for the outline and for every page file.
- **deck_audit_clean**: `slides audit` returns no `detail.issues`, or every remaining issue is listed in `deck_review`.
- **deck_render_reviewed**: the slides were rendered to images and actually looked at; a host that cannot view images records this as not-tested.
- **deck_facts_sourced**: every figure traces to the user's material or a search result, and illustrative numbers are labelled.

## Sources

- AI intent mapping: genoffice skill → office.presentation-creation, from its "Designing a deck", "Which command" and "Before you say done" sections. The same skill also yields the intents of `office-authoring` and `office-files`.
- Source: genoffice (genspark-ai/genoffice@4b55db9e, release v0.12.852) — `skills/genoffice/SKILL.md` (skill 2.68.0, cli >=0.9.0)
- Runtime dependency: the GenOffice app and its `genoffice` command line (Apache-2.0), not bundled by Muro; the capability installs it from the official releases when it is missing.
- Not adopted: `search`, `image` and `media` give no standalone intent; they are optional, data-leaving steps of this pipeline. The skill, MCP and CLI installation or registration commands are dropped.
- Hooks: the selected SKILL.md defines none. The rest of the repository (app, packaging, CLAUDE.md, .github) was not inspected for hooks.
- Harmonization 2026-11-12 (claude-design-system-prompt intake): `html-deck` builds a presentation as a web page. The two are alternatives by wanted format with different outputs; a request that names no format stays here, and this intent already excludes an HTML slideshow.
- Harmonized by: prompts/harmonizer.md — pipeline kept as written.
- Changes for coexistence (ADR-0017): the frontmatter `name` and `description` are not carried (the coordinator classifies by meaning and this body is not registered as a skill); the commands that install or register the source itself (`skill list`, `skill install`, `skill path`, `mcp install`, `mcp uninstall`, `mcp list`, `install-cli`) are not followed (a capability never installs the source plugin); step 1 adds the install of a missing engine from the official releases and "do not simulate", where the source assumes GenOffice is installed and gives no method (ADR-0007); the source's "Report the path" goes through `## Output handoff` (the coordinator owns outputs); the render check may be recorded as not-tested on a host that cannot view images (a step that host cannot run); editing an existing deck, the workbook and document paths, `merge`, `open` with a target and `selection` are run by `office-files` and `office-authoring`, not in this step (one capability per step); `search`, `image` and `media` are followed only as steps of this pipeline, not as standalone uses (dropped in `delivery.json`).

# Office Authoring (new document, workbook or PDF)

Creates a new Word document, Excel workbook or PDF as a real file with the locally installed `genoffice` engine, then checks it and looks at it before reporting.

## Behavior

The full version is `<package_root>/scripts/genoffice/SKILL.source.md`. It wins where this body differs, except for the changes listed in the Sources section. Open only the section a step points to.

1. **Check the engine.** Run `genoffice --version` first. If the command is not found, read the one line in `~/.genoffice/launcher` (Windows: `%USERPROFILE%\.genoffice\launcher`), which GenOffice writes on every start, and run `"<dir>/genoffice"` from bash or `"<dir>\genoffice.cmd"` from PowerShell / cmd, quoted, in place of `genoffice`; the default locations when that file is missing are in the original's opening paragraph. If GenOffice is not installed, install it: say in one line what is installed and from where (the release for this platform from https://github.com/genspark-ai/genoffice/releases), run it, then confirm with `genoffice --version`. If the installer needs the user or fails, say which step is theirs and stop this delivery; do not simulate a file or build it another way. Always add `--json` when a program reads the output; read `status`, `error`, `suggestion` and `detail`, never parse `message`.
2. **Prepare the content** as a file the engine reads: Markdown or a restricted-HTML fragment for a document; CSV or JSON (a 2-D array or `{sheets:[{name,rows}]}`) for a workbook, where `"=..."` cells are formulas. You read the user's source material yourself (md, txt, csv, pdf, images directly); when it is a docx, xlsx or pptx, open "Reading the user's files" in the original for the CLI command. Take figures and wording from that material; never `cat` or `unzip` an Office file.
3. **Create.**
   - Document: `genoffice create --type docx --from <text.md | fragment.html> --out <path>`. Local images a Markdown file references by relative path are embedded.
   - Workbook: `genoffice create --type xlsx --from <data.csv | table.json> [--header] [--decimal ,] --out <path>`. `--header` freezes row 1 and filters the range; without it the first row is data.
   - PDF: `genoffice create --type pdf --from <document> --out <path>`, from the md or html written in this step or from the docx or xlsx made in this step. A PDF of a file the user already has is a format conversion (`office-files`).
4. **Refine with ops.** Workbook: `sheet apply --ops` for formats and charts. Before writing ops run `genoffice guide <domain>` (`guide <domain> <op> --json` for one op's schema), then write the ops JSON yourself. Run `genoffice <domain> apply --dry-run` when the batch is large. Apply is atomic by default: a rejected op comes back as `op_rejected` with the executor's usage line and the file is untouched; fix that op and resend the whole batch. Open the Word or Excel item of "Behaviour to know" and "Limits" in the original when the ops insert or delete blocks, rows or columns, or add fields, charts, pivots, sections or tables: they give the ordering and index rules inside a batch.
5. **Check.** Workbook: `sheet check book.xlsx --json` shows no `formula_error`, `missing_sheet_ref`, `number_overflow` (apply the `set_col_width` suggestions). Document: `docs check report.docx --json` shows no `broken_ref`, `placeholder_left`, `field_not_evaluated` that you can fix. Both exit 0 whether or not they found something: the findings are in `detail.issues[]` with a stable `code`, a `path` and, when possible, a `suggest` op to pass to `apply` as is.
6. **Look.** Workbook: `render book.xlsx --out shots --json` and look at the sheet PNG. Document: `render report.docx --out shots --json` and look at page 1 and the last. Report the `.xlsx` path, naming uncached formulas if any, or the `.docx` path.

## Output handoff

Return `office_file` (every path written) and `office_review` (check findings, what was looked at, warnings) as JSON strings. For a mapped step, submit them through the coordinator's `record` command with the step's `map_id` and `capability`. Do not edit `<state_dir>/map.md` or `<state_dir>/state.json`; the coordinator is their only writer.

## Specifics

- `create --type docx --from` is not for a real web page: that is `convert page.html --to docx` (html2docx). A restricted-HTML fragment with `<formula>` goes through `create --type docx --from fragment.html`. Tags outside the restricted set are stripped silently.
- CSV import: a `sep=;` first line is honoured and removed, ISO dates become real dates, `--decimal ,` reads `1.234,5` as 1234.5.
- Formulas the local engine cannot evaluate (FILTER, SORT, UNIQUE, LET, LAMBDA …) are written without a cached value: the `formulas_not_cached` warning lists them and `sheet read` shows the formula and no value until Excel opens the file. Not an error; name them in the report.
- PAGE / NUMPAGES / AUTHOR-style field results are placeholders Word recomputes on open (`docs check` reports them as info); say so when you hand over the file.
- `→pdf`, `docx→html`, `html→docx`, `create --type pdf` and `render` run a hidden GenOffice process per call (1–6 s, up to 180 s timeout, safe to run concurrently) and need GenOffice installed or `GENOFFICE_APP_BIN` pointing at it.
- `create`, `convert` and `image` never overwrite (exit 2, `output_exists`): pick another name, or `--force` when the user asked for replacement. If `GENOFFICE_ALLOWED_ROOTS` is set, genoffice reads and writes only inside those directories (exit 2 otherwise); stay within them.
- Every command runs headless on the app's own engines; only `search`, `image` and `media` send data off the machine, to the provider configured in GenOffice. This capability's paths do not use those three.
- Do not run `genoffice open` unless the user asks to see the file in GenOffice.
- When a command returns `status: "error"`: branch on `error`, do what `suggestion` says, then resend the whole batch. Open the table in "When a command fails" for the next command of that `error` value. A successful result may still carry `warnings[]`: read them, report what matters, do not retry.

## Checks

- **engine_check_clean**: `sheet check` shows no `formula_error`, `missing_sheet_ref` or `number_overflow`, or `docs check` shows no `broken_ref`, `placeholder_left` or `field_not_evaluated` that can be fixed; each remaining finding is listed in `office_review`.
- **office_render_reviewed**: the file was rendered to images and actually looked at; a host that cannot view images records this as not-tested.
- **uncached_values_disclosed**: uncached formulas and fields that the Office app recomputes on open are named in the report.
- **content_from_user_material**: figures, names and dates trace to the user's material; nothing is invented.

## Sources

- AI intent mapping: genoffice skill → office.document-creation and office.spreadsheet-creation, from its "Commands", "Which command", "Behaviour to know" and "Before you say done" sections.
- Source: genoffice (genspark-ai/genoffice@4b55db9e, release v0.12.852) — `skills/genoffice/SKILL.md` (skill 2.68.0, cli >=0.9.0)
- Runtime dependency: the GenOffice app and its `genoffice` command line (Apache-2.0), not bundled by Muro; the capability installs it from the official releases when it is missing.
- Hooks: the selected SKILL.md defines none. The rest of the repository was not inspected for hooks.
- Harmonized by: prompts/harmonizer.md — document and workbook creation share one role because they share the create → check → render flow; deck creation is a separate role with its own pipeline.

# Office Files (read, convert and edit existing files)

Works on Office and PDF files that already exist: reads their structure and text, converts formats and applies structured edits through the `genoffice` engine, keeping the file's own design.

## Behavior

The full version is `<package_root>/scripts/genoffice/SKILL.source.md`. It wins where this body differs, except for the changes listed in the Sources section. Open only the section a step points to.

1. **Check the engine.** Run `genoffice --version` first. If the command is not found, read the one line in `~/.genoffice/launcher` (Windows: `%USERPROFILE%\.genoffice\launcher`), which GenOffice writes on every start, and run `"<dir>/genoffice"` from bash or `"<dir>\genoffice.cmd"` from PowerShell / cmd, quoted, in place of `genoffice`; the default locations when that file is missing are in the original's opening paragraph. If GenOffice is not installed, install it: say in one line what is installed and from where (the release for this platform from https://github.com/genspark-ai/genoffice/releases), run it, then confirm with `genoffice --version`. If the installer needs the user or fails, say which step is theirs and stop this delivery; do not simulate a result or build it another way. Always add `--json` when a program reads the output; read `status`, `error`, `suggestion` and `detail`, never parse `message`.
2. **Read first.** `genoffice info <file>` or `genoffice <domain> read --json` gives the structure: block indexes (docx), `s_<n>` / `e_*` ids and EMU geometry (pptx), sheet names and cell values (xlsx). `sheet read` without `--range` stops at 500 rows and says `truncated: true`: run `--stats` first to size a workbook, `--cols` / `--max-rows` to page through it, `--where formula` for the formulas alone. Use `pdf read --range a-b` when you cannot open the PDF yourself (password-protected, or page sizes and metadata are needed). Never `cat` or `unzip` an Office file. For other read flags (comments, revisions, styles, sections, notes, text caps) open the command's row in "Commands".
3. **Pick the route.**
   - *Source material or a question:* `convert --to md/csv` or `<domain> read --full --json`, not `render` (pixels, not text). Open "Reading the user's files" for the command per format. Nothing is written to the file.
   - *Format change:* `genoffice convert <file> --to <fmt> [--out <path>] [--force]`; the supported pairs are in the `convert` row of "Commands". Not for a content change: edit first, convert after.
   - *Edit:* run `genoffice guide <domain>` (`guide <domain> <op> --json` for one op's schema), then write the ops JSON yourself and run `genoffice <domain> apply <file> --ops <file>`. One cell fix in a workbook: `sheet apply --cells`. Before writing ops, open the item of "Behaviour to know" for that domain (Word, Excel or PowerPoint), and "Limits" for pivots, sparklines, conditional formats and data validation. For a deck follow "Editing an existing deck": use ops, not the staged pipeline, and keep the deck's own design.
   - *Fill a template:* `genoffice merge <template.docx|pptx|xlsx> --data <values.json | inline JSON> --out <path> [--force] [--strict]`; open the `merge` row of "Commands" to read `detail.unresolved_placeholders[]`.
   - *Redline two Word versions:* `genoffice docs compare <original.docx> <revised.docx> --out <redline.docx>`.
   - *External workbook links:* `genoffice sheet links <xlsx> [--update] [--break indices]`, row in "Commands".
   - *Show or point in the editor:* `genoffice open <file> [--slide n [--el e_12] | --block n | --range [Sheet!]B2:D5 | --page n]`, only when the user asks to see it there; `genoffice selection <file> --json` resolves "this one" / "here" before editing.
4. **Apply safely.** Run `apply --dry-run` when the batch is large. Apply is atomic by default: a rejected op comes back as `op_rejected` with the executor's usage line, the file is untouched and `detail.batch` is `{total, applied: 0, failed, skipped}`; fix that op and resend the whole batch. `--best-effort` applies every op that can apply and `--stop-on-error` applies in order up to the first rejection; both write the file and answer `status: "partial"` with exit 0, the lost ops in `detail.failures` and the counts in `detail.batch`. Check `status`, not only the exit code.
5. **Verify, then report the output path.** Three lines per artifact, every time (check, look, report): open the artifact's row in the table of `Before you say "done"`. `check` and `audit` exit 0 whether or not they found something; the findings are in `detail.issues[]`, with a `suggest` op when possible. After a deck edit run `genoffice slides audit deck.pptx --slide n --json` (a longer sentence in the same box overflows), apply the `suggest` ops it returns, then render once more and look.

## Output handoff

Return `file_reading` (what was read: structure, ids, sizes) and `file_result` (paths written, batch status and warnings, or that the request was read-only and no file changed) as JSON strings. For a mapped step, submit them through the coordinator's `record` command with the step's `map_id` and `capability`. Do not edit `<state_dir>/map.md` or `<state_dir>/state.json`; the coordinator is their only writer.

## Specifics

- Structural edits renumber: new `e_*` ids after `addElement`, `s_*` after adding slides, docx block indexes after `insert_content` / `delete_blocks`; ids of edited slide elements change too. Inside one batch indexes are live; before the next batch run `read` again. Revision ids are positional: read again after any edit before `accept_changes` / `reject_changes`.
- `--slide n` of `slides read/audit/render/replace` and op targets `{ "slide": n }` are 0-based, `render --page n` is 1-based, docx block indexes are 0-based. `sheet apply` addresses sheets by the current tab name in the file, spelled as in the tab.
- **Keep the original.** `apply` edits in place unless `--out` is given; write with `--out` when the user wants the original kept. `create`, `convert` and `image` never overwrite and `apply --out` onto an existing file refuses (exit 2, `output_exists`): pick another name, or `--force` when the user asked for replacement. A file open in a GenOffice tab makes `apply` refuse (exit 2, `file_open_in_gui`): ask the user to close the tab, or use `--out other.ext`; `--force` only if the user accepts the editor may overwrite it.
- Losses to report: `convert pptx→pdf` has no text layer; `convert docx→md` drops images (`detail.skipped`), so use `docs read --full` when you need every word; scanned PDF pages have empty text (`convert --to docx` runs OCR). `docs findReplace` skips table cells (use `replace_blocks` on the table block), and unknown HTML tags in `insert_content` are stripped silently (stay inside the restricted set of `guide docs`).
- Excel ops that still need the live editor (`refresh_pivot`, edits to session-created tables and shapes) are refused with the reason.
- Changing text, a picture or one slide is not restyling the whole deck: that is the `applyTheme` op, or a rebuild through the staged path, which is a new deck by `office-deck`. `slides replace --slide n --spec` is for decks the staged pipeline built, not for restyling a deck the user brought.
- `file_not_open_in_gui`: `selection` and `open --el` need the file in a tab; run `genoffice open <file>` first, then ask the user to select. `outside_allowed_roots`: stay inside `GENOFFICE_ALLOWED_ROOTS`, do not try another location. `resource_limit`: do not retry, tell the user.
- Any other `error`: branch on it, do what `suggestion` says, then resend the whole batch; open the table in "When a command fails" for the next command of that value. A successful result may still carry `warnings[]`: read them, report what matters, do not retry.
- **Data leaving the machine:** every command runs headless on the app's own engines; only `search`, `image` and `media` send data off the machine (the query or the referenced file), to the provider configured in GenOffice.

## Checks

- **structure_read_before_edit**: ids, block indexes, sheet names or ranges used by the ops come from a read of the current file, repeated after any structural edit.
- **batch_status_verified**: the result's `status` was read; a `partial` batch lists its lost ops in `file_result`.
- **post_edit_check_clean**: `slides audit`, `sheet check` or `docs check` after the edit shows no new issue, or each one is listed.
- **original_preserved**: no file was overwritten or forced without the user's request; a read-only request changed nothing.
- **conversion_loss_reported**: dropped images, a missing text layer, uncached formulas and other `warnings[]` are reported to the user.

## Sources

- AI intent mapping: genoffice skill → office.file-editing, office.format-conversion, office.content-extraction and office.editor-handoff, from its "Commands", "Which command", "Workflow", "Pitfalls", "Reading the user's files", "Editing an existing deck" and "Path rules" sections.
- Source: genoffice (genspark-ai/genoffice@4b55db9e, release v0.12.852) — `skills/genoffice/SKILL.md` (skill 2.68.0, cli >=0.9.0)
- Runtime dependency: the GenOffice app and its `genoffice` command line (Apache-2.0), not bundled by Muro; the capability installs it from the official releases when it is missing.
- Not adopted: `skill list|install|path`, `mcp install|uninstall|list` and `install-cli` (installation and registration). The `genoffice mcp` server is only an equivalent way to reach the same commands; the app's own MCP server for documents open in the editor is not used.
- Hooks: the selected SKILL.md defines none. The rest of the repository was not inspected for hooks. Side effects of the tool itself: an audit log line per command and the launcher path file written by the app.
- Harmonized by: prompts/harmonizer.md — reading, converting and editing share one role because each starts from an existing file and the same read step.
- Changes for coexistence (ADR-0017): the frontmatter `name` and `description` are not carried (the coordinator classifies by meaning and this body is not registered as a skill); the commands that install or register the source itself (`skill list`, `skill install`, `skill path`, `mcp install`, `mcp uninstall`, `mcp list`, `install-cli`) are not followed (a capability never installs the source plugin); step 1 adds the install of a missing engine from the official releases and "do not simulate", where the source assumes GenOffice is installed and gives no method (ADR-0007); the source's "Report the path" goes through `## Output handoff` (the coordinator owns outputs); the render check may be recorded as not-tested on a host that cannot view images (a step that host cannot run); the deck pipeline and the creation of a new document, workbook or PDF from content are run by `office-deck` and `office-authoring`, not in this step (one capability per step); the source's "or rebuild through the staged path" for restyling a whole deck is a handoff to `office-deck`, not done here; `search`, `image` and `media` are not standalone uses (dropped in `delivery.json`).

# Interactive Explainer

Produces one `index.html` in the style of distill.pub: serif text, a sticky sidebar and canvas figures the reader operates, built in stages and never delivered with an unverified factual claim. `<ET>` below stands for `<package_root>/scripts/explain-this/skills`. The packaged originals under it are the full version: open what a step names when the task needs it; where this body differs the original wins, except for the changes listed in the Sources section.

## Behavior

1. **Intake.** Open only the reference of the branch that fits:
   - files, a URL or pasted text: `<ET>/creating-explainers/references/intake-from-files.md`. The provided documents are the source of truth.
   - only a topic: `<ET>/creating-explainers/references/intake-from-research.md`. If web search is unavailable, ask the user to paste sources; do not write from memory.
   - files plus a topic they do not cover: both references; the files are the spine, research is supporting, and there is one outline and one article.
   - a codebase or source files: `<ET>/explaining-codebases/references/code-intake.md`. Confirm the angle with the user (architecture overview or one mechanism), state the spine as one sentence, and quote real snippets of 5-20 lines, each tagged `path:line`. One subsystem or one mechanism per article.
2. **Research-time fact-check (required if you researched).** Before the outline, confirm that each gathered source exists and supports the points it will be used for; drop or replace any that does not hold up. In a mixed intake this covers the researched sources only: the user's files are ground truth. A codebase explainer with no research skips this step.
3. **Outline, then stop for approval.** Show the title, subtitle, section list with one-line summaries, and a numbered figure list saying what each figure shows and how the reader interacts with it, in the outline format of the intake reference in use (a codebase outline adds the snippet list). This is the only planned pause: after it, show progress and do not ask permission to continue unless something is genuinely ambiguous.
4. **Scaffold.** Copy `<ET>/creating-explainers/assets/article-template.html` to `<article-folder>/index.html` and fill its `{{PLACEHOLDERS}}`; do not rebuild the structure from scratch. `<ET>/creating-explainers/references/template-walkthrough.md` says what each block is and where content goes; pick the accent colors from `<ET>/creating-explainers/references/color-palettes.md`.
5. **Prose pass.** Read `<ET>/creating-explainers/references/voice-and-style.md` before writing prose, then write every section with figure placeholders. In short: second person; paragraphs of 80-180 words; no bullet lists in body prose; open with a concrete scene or tension, not a definition; captions say what to look for; 3-5 `.callout` per article; never an em-dash.
6. **Figures pass.** Aim for 3-5 figures, each paying off something the prose has just set up; none is decorative. Each is a self-contained IIFE with its state in closure variables, not globals, and the one shared utility is `initCanvas(id)`, always used for canvas sizing. Open the section of `<ET>/creating-explainers/references/figure-archetypes.md` for the archetype you implement (always for 3D rotation, whose correctness details it handles), and for code figures also `<ET>/explaining-codebases/references/code-figure-archetypes.md`.
7. **Post-draft fact-check (required, blocking).** Extract every checkable claim of the finished article with its location, read the source passage that backs it (for a codebase explainer, the actual code at the exact path and line, for every behaviour claim, snippet and architecture claim), and give each a verdict: `supported`, `needs-source`, `unsupported` or `contradicted`. Resolve all that are not `supported`: add support, correct to the source, soften to clearly-labeled interpretation when the statement really is interpretive, or cut. Write the report in the format of `<ET>/fact-checking-explainers/references/verification-report-format.md`, apply the fixes and re-run on the changed claims. Deliver only on `PASS`. When unsure what must be checked, open "What Counts as a Checkable Claim" in `<ET>/fact-checking-explainers/SKILL.source.md`.
8. **Polish.** Run every item of the "Quality Checklist" section of `<ET>/creating-explainers/SKILL.source.md` and fix each failing one before delivery; the step is complete only when all pass. To test locally, run `python3 -m http.server 8000` from the directory containing the file and open it in a browser, if browser tooling is available. If it is not, at minimum grep for `getElementById` calls without matching IDs, canvas IDs referenced before declaration, and `initCanvas` not defined.

## Output handoff

Resolve `<package_root>` with the `package_root` returned beside these instructions, never against the consumer project. Return `explainer_outline` (the approved outline and figure list), `explainer_file` (the index.html path) and `explainer_claims` (the claim report and its PASS or FAIL line) as JSON strings. For a mapped step, submit them through the coordinator's `record` command with the step's `map_id` and `capability`. Do not edit `<state_dir>/map.md` or `<state_dir>/state.json`; the coordinator is their only writer.

## Specifics

- Non-negotiable: zero dependencies (no npm, bundler, React, D3, Three.js or Tailwind; vanilla HTML, inline CSS and vanilla JS only) and one file per article, with all CSS in a single `<style>` block in `<head>` and all JS at the bottom of `<body>`. The only external network requests are Google Fonts. This overrides the project's own frontend stack; the article folder stands alone.
- Keep the template's Google Fonts link (Crimson Pro and JetBrains Mono): do not remove it and do not add other fonts.
- Figures are hand-coded Canvas, not SVG libraries or images; 3D uses custom projection, z-sorting and lighting.
- For code: never tidy a snippet into something the repo does not contain; build diagrams from the actual imports and call sites; note when code is generated and prefer explaining its source.
- The article has no dependency to install; only the optional viewing browser may be installed, and only when none exists.

## Checks

- **outline_approved_by_user**: the user accepted the outline and figure list before scaffolding.
- **single_file_no_dependencies**: the article folder holds one index.html with inline CSS and JS and no external script or stylesheet other than the fonts link.
- **figures_render_and_respond**: every figure draws without console errors and every control changes it; a host without a browser records this as not-tested.
- **claims_gate_passed**: the claim report ends with `PASS`, every row `supported`.

## Sources

# Explainer Fact-Check

No explainer ships with an unverified factual claim: every checkable claim traces to a source that supports it, is corrected to match the source, or is cut. The packaged original, `<package_root>/scripts/explain-this/skills/fact-checking-explainers/SKILL.source.md`, is the full version of this procedure: open the section a step names when the task needs it, and where this body differs the original wins, except for the changes listed in the Sources section.

## Behavior

1. **Extract** every checkable claim with its location (section, figure caption, or `file:line` for code). Checkable: numbers, dates, measurements, percentages; names, attributions, who did or built what; direct quotes; historical events and their order; performance results and benchmarks; mechanism claims ("X uses Y", "X causes Y", "X is faster than Y because Z"). Not flagged: clearly-labeled interpretation or opinion, analogies and illustrative scenarios the reader knows are illustrative, the author's framing and transitions. When unsure, treat it as checkable and verify it.
2. **Find the support.** For each claim, locate the passage in the cited source that backs it and read it; for a codebase explainer, open the actual code at the exact path and line. A citation existing is not support, and for code a name or a comment is not evidence: read the implementation. The original's "Red Flags" and "Rationalization Table" list the thoughts that mean stop and verify: open them when a claim seems too obvious to check.
3. **Assign a verdict:** `supported` (a source passage directly backs the claim), `needs-source` (plausible but no citation yet), `unsupported` (no source backs it) or `contradicted` (a source says otherwise). Only `supported` is allowed at delivery.
4. **Report** in the format of `<package_root>/scripts/explain-this/skills/fact-checking-explainers/references/verification-report-format.md` (open it for the column notes): one table row per checkable claim with the columns `#`, Claim (quoted), Location, Verdict, Source / evidence, Severity, Recommended fix. Severity is `high` for a numeric, named, dated or mechanism error a reader could act on or repeat, `low` for a minor imprecision that does not change the reader's understanding. After the table, one line: `PASS` only if every row is `supported`; otherwise `FAIL` with a count of unresolved rows by verdict, for example `FAIL - 1 contradicted, 2 unsupported, 1 needs-source`.
5. **Offer the fixes.** Present the report to the user and offer to apply the fixes: add support from a source passage, correct the claim to what the source actually says, soften to clearly-labeled interpretation only if the statement is genuinely interpretive rather than factual, or cut it. After the user accepts, apply them and re-run on the changed claims.

## Output handoff

Resolve `<package_root>` with the `package_root` returned beside these instructions, never against the consumer project. Return `verification_report` (the table) and `verification_verdict` (the PASS or FAIL line, and whether fixes were applied) as JSON strings. For a mapped step, submit them through the coordinator's `record` command with the step's `map_id` and `capability`. Do not edit `<state_dir>/map.md` or `<state_dir>/state.json`; the coordinator is their only writer.

## Specifics

- Verifying means checking an actual source in this session. Memory, plausibility, background knowledge and deadline pressure are signals to run the loop, not reasons to skip it.
- Numbers, dates and names are exact or they are wrong; "roughly" or "about" attached to a specific number is a signal to re-open the source.
- If sources disagree, the disagreement belongs in the article.
- An unresolved `needs-source`, `unsupported` or `contradicted` claim keeps the report at FAIL; a caveat does not make an unsupported factual claim deliverable.
- A source that cannot be opened (no web access, missing file) leaves its claims `needs-source`; say which ones.
- No runtime dependency is installed by this capability.

## Checks

- **every_claim_has_a_verdict**: each checkable claim in the article has one row and one of the four verdicts.
- **evidence_opened_this_session**: every `supported` row quotes the passage or code that was actually read.
- **verdict_matches_rows**: the final line is `PASS` only when all rows are `supported`; otherwise `FAIL` with the counts.

## Sources

- AI intent mapping: fact-checking-explainers → explainer.fact-check (its "on request" use). Its research-time and post-draft gates are steps of `interactive-explainer`.

- Changes for coexistence (ADR-0017):
  - The original's frontmatter triggers and "When to Use" list are not followed: routing is the coordinator's, by meaning, from this capability's intent.
  - Only the original's "On request" use is applied here; "The Two Gates" and the "As a gate" report rule are steps 2 and 7 of `interactive-explainer` (one capability per step).
  - The original's process step 4 "Resolve" comes after the report and on the user's acceptance (step 5 here): the original's own direct-request rule, and the article is the user's.

  - Added "A source that cannot be opened ... leaves its claims `needs-source`; say which ones": `web-research` is optional, and a claim whose source was not opened must not be reported `supported`.
- Runtime dependency: none.

# HTML Explanation

Answers a request to explain or understand something with one rich HTML page instead of a chat message: background, intuition, walkthrough and a quiz, read top to bottom. The packaged original, `<package_root>/scripts/open-paper-skills/skills/explain-anything-html/SKILL.source.md`, is one page and is the full version of this method: read it before writing. It wins where this body differs from it, except for the changes listed in the Sources section.

## Behavior

1. **Take in the subject.** Read the paper, post, article or documentation the user names, or pin down the concept. Explore the source material broadly and, where useful, the related work or prerequisite ideas it builds on. When an earlier step recorded `literature_findings`, start from the text it fetched.
2. **Write four sections on one long page.**
   - **Background**: the existing context relevant to the subject. How much the reader knows is unknown, so include a deep background for beginners, noting that a reader already familiar can skip it, then a narrower background directly relevant to the subject.
   - **Intuition**: the essence, not the full details: the paper's central idea, the post's key argument, the heart of the concept. Use concrete examples with toy data, and figures and diagrams liberally.
   - **Walkthrough**: a high-level walkthrough of the substance: the methods, arguments, results or key sections. Group and order the material so it is understood, not in the source's order when another order explains it better.
   - **Quiz**: five questions that test whether the reader has actually understood. Medium difficulty: hard enough that answering needs the substance, never gotchas. They are interactive multiple-choice questions: a click tells the reader whether the answer is correct and gives feedback.
3. **Format.** One self-contained HTML file with its CSS and JavaScript inside. One long page with section headers and a table of contents; no tabs for the top-level structure. Basic responsive styling, so the page can be read on a phone, is welcome too.
4. **Voice.** The clarity and flow of Martin Kleppmann: engaging, in classic style, with smooth transitions between sections.
5. **Diagrams.** Ideally pick a small number of diagram families and reuse them through the page for the various cases. Useful kinds: a schematic or conceptual diagram of the key idea, of the states before and after, or of how the pieces relate, concrete with example values where possible; a system diagram of the data flow or of the relation between components or steps, with example data in it. Never an ASCII diagram: simple HTML designs for diagrams, HTML lists for lists.
6. **Preformatted text.** Code blocks, equations and any preformatted text go in `<pre>` tags. A custom styled `div` used in their place must have `white-space: pre-wrap` in its CSS, or the browser collapses all its newlines into one line. Before saving, scan each code block in the HTML source and confirm its CSS includes `white-space: pre` or `pre-wrap`.
7. **Callouts.** Use callouts for key concepts or definitions, important edge cases and the like.
8. **Save outside the project.** Put the file in a global place on the user's computer, outside the code repository, under a name that always starts with today's date as `YYYY-MM-DD-`: that keeps the files sorted by time and out of version control. The source's example is `/tmp/2026-01-12-explanation-<slug>.html`; on a system with no `/tmp` use its temporary folder. When a file of that name already exists (the same subject, explained earlier that day), that is not a reason to stop: read it first when the user asked to redo that page, otherwise keep it and add a short suffix to the new name (`-2`). Give the user the full path.

## Output handoff

Resolve `<package_root>` with the `package_root` returned beside these instructions, never against the consumer project. Return `explanation_file` (the full path of the HTML file) as a JSON string. For a mapped step, submit it through the coordinator's `record` command with the step's `map_id` and `capability`. Do not edit `<state_dir>/map.md` or `<state_dir>/state.json`; the coordinator is their only writer.

## Specifics

- This method has no outline to approve, no fixed number of figures and no claim gate: those belong to `interactive-explainer`, which is another capability and never runs in the same plan.
- Nothing is installed: the page needs only a browser to be read.

## Checks

- **four_sections_one_long_page**: Background (the beginner part marked as skippable, then the narrow part), Intuition, Walkthrough and Quiz are all there, on one long page with section headers and a table of contents and no top-level tabs.
- **quiz_five_questions_give_feedback**: the quiz has five multiple-choice questions, and on a click the page says whether the answer is correct and gives feedback.
- **single_dated_file_outside_repo**: one self-contained HTML file, CSS and JavaScript inside, saved outside the code repository under a name that starts with today's date as `YYYY-MM-DD-`.
- **preformatted_blocks_keep_whitespace**: every code block, equation or preformatted text is a `<pre>` or has `white-space: pre` or `pre-wrap`, confirmed in the HTML source before saving, and no diagram is ASCII.

## Sources

- AI intent mapping: explain-anything-html → explanation.html-page, its one outcome. Its trigger ("even if they don't explicitly ask for HTML") is the intent's meaning.
- Source: open-paper-skills (pengqianhan/open-paper-skills@f85fd3dc, head) — `skills/explain-anything-html/SKILL.md`, the whole skill, packaged unchanged as `<package_root>/scripts/open-paper-skills/skills/explain-anything-html/SKILL.source.md`.
- Origin of the text, as the skill states it: "Adapted from `explain-diff-html`, which is based on Geoffrey Litt's original skill" (gist `geoffreylitt/a29df1b5f9865506e8952488eac3d524`). The licence verified is the repository's MIT. The gist carries no licence statement (read on 2026-11-18): open for the owner.

# Paper Search

One script searches every literature source the user has switched on, in parallel, and returns one JSON shape; its `fetch` reads one paper through the user's read order. `$PS` below is `<package_root>/scripts/open-paper-skills/skills/paper-search/scripts/paper_search.py`. The packaged original, `<package_root>/scripts/open-paper-skills/skills/paper-search/SKILL.source.md`, is the full version of this method and wins where this body differs from it, except for the changes listed in the Sources section. Open it only where a step below says so.

## Behavior

1. **Run from the user's project.** The script finds the switch file `memory/paper-sources.json` by walking up from the working directory, so work from inside the user's project. bioRxiv and PubMed start switched off and every other source starts on; a source the file leaves out keeps that default. `uv run $PS sources` shows which sources are on.
2. **A source that is off is off on every route.** Reach literature through `$PS`, and do not reach a switched-off source another way either: MCP connectors, other skills (the other capabilities of this package included) and web fetches. When the evidence needs a source that is off, say so and let the user decide.
3. **Search.** `uv run $PS search "<query>"` searches every source that is on; repeat `--source <name>` to narrow. Pick the sources that fit the field: machine learning through `alphaxiv`, `huggingface` and `pwc`; journal and cross-disciplinary work through `openalex`; biology through `biorxiv` and `pubmed`; an exact title, author or arXiv category through `arxiv` with a fielded query such as `ti:"context language models"` (`ti:`, `au:`, `abs:`, `cat:`). Open the table in the original's "Search" section when you need what each source covers or which extra fields (votes, citations, code) it returns.
   - `--mode semantic` (default) or `keyword`: alphaXiv embedding or full-text keyword search, PwC hybrid or keyword, arXiv all-words or exact phrase; other sources ignore it. Use `keyword` for exact method names, acronyms, benchmarks and title phrases.
   - `--published-after` / `--published-before YYYY-MM-DD`: inclusive window. Supply one only when the question asks for a period.
   - `--limit N`: results per source (default 10; PwC caps at 25).
4. **Read the result.** The script prints `{query, searched, disabled, errors, results}`. Each result has `source`, `id` (an arXiv id, a DOI, an OpenAlex `W…` id, a PMID or a PwC catalog id), `title`, `url` and whatever else its source provides.
   - Results interleave the sources rank by rank. A paper several sources found appears once, under the first source, with the others in `also_in`; it keeps that source's `votes` and takes missing fields such as `code` from the rest.
   - `errors` names each source that failed. Report a failed source as unsearched, never as evidence that no such literature exists; the same holds for an empty result. Exit 0: at least one source answered; 1: every searched source failed; 2: invalid use, including asking for a source that is off.
   - Cite only papers the results or a follow-up read actually returned.
5. **Read a paper.** `uv run $PS fetch <id>` takes an arXiv id or URL, a DOI, an OpenAlex `W…` id or a PubMed id and routes it by shape; `--via <source>` reads through one source only; `--report` gives alphaXiv's overview of about 10 KB, for skimming.
   - An arXiv paper is read from each source in the read order (default `huggingface`, `alphaxiv`, `arxiv`), skipping switched-off sources, until one returns a complete text: at least 5,000 characters with a heading such as Introduction or Method. A cut-short text (the lone figure caption Hugging Face serves for some fresh submissions) falls through to the next source.
   - The text goes to a file (`--out`, default under the system temp directory); stdout is a JSON report with `tried` (each source's outcome), `source`, `url`, `file`, `chars` and `metadata` from arXiv, else Hugging Face. Read the file in parts and cite the `source` and `url` the report names.
   - Exit 1: no source returned a complete text; report the `tried` outcomes and the `pdf` link and let the user decide. `--via` or `--report` through a switched-off source exits 2.
   - A DOI, OpenAlex id or PMID returns its record (no full text) from OpenAlex, bioRxiv or PubMed, under that source's switch; follow its `url` or `doi` for the text.
   - When the host has a logged-in alphaXiv connector, use it to put questions to a paper's PDF. It belongs to the `alphaxiv` source and follows that switch.
6. **Keys.** Each user brings optional keys: `OPENALEX_API_KEY` (OpenAlex and bioRxiv), `NCBI_API_KEY` (PubMed), `HF_TOKEN` (Hugging Face); alphaXiv and PwC need none. The script reads them from the environment, else from the gitignored `.env` of the user's project, beside its `memory/` folder. `uv run $PS keys` shows which are set. A rate-limited source (`HTTP 429`) comes back naming the key that lifts the limit: relay that next step to the user, who edits `.env` or has `keys --set NAME` store the value it reads from stdin. Keep key values out of commits, prompts and logs.
7. **Switches belong to the user.** Change a switch only on the user's word: `uv run $PS sources --disable pubmed`, `uv run $PS sources --enable pubmed --json`. The read order is the user's choice too: `sources --read-order alphaxiv,huggingface,arxiv` sets it, and a source left out of it is not read through by `fetch` while search still uses it. Both rewrite `memory/paper-sources.json`, a tracked file; commit it with the change that motivated it. In a project with no switch file the script answers `no memory/paper-sources.json above the working directory; pass --config`: pass `--config <project>/memory/paper-sources.json` to create it there.

## Output handoff

Resolve `<package_root>` with the `package_root` returned beside these instructions, never against the consumer project. Return `literature_findings` as one JSON string: the query or id, the sources searched, the sources that failed or are off, and the papers kept (title, id, source, url, why each matters) or the path and source of the fetched text. For a mapped step, submit it through the coordinator's `record` command with the step's `map_id` and `capability`. Do not edit `<state_dir>/map.md` or `<state_dir>/state.json`; the coordinator is their only writer.

## Specifics

- Open "Known source behaviour" in the original's "Read the result" section when a search is rate-limited or slow, or a date window returns odd results: it covers the PwC limit of 10 hybrid searches per minute per IP (bursts need `--mode keyword`) and `PWC_MCP_URL`, the Hugging Face and PubMed date windows, and arXiv's one request every three seconds.
- Runtime dependency: `uv`, or Python 3.11+ already present. The source runs every command as `uv run $PS ...`. When `uv` is missing and wanted, install it from astral.sh (user scope) and say so in one line; `uv run` then installs the optional `truststore` named in the script header. When `uv` is missing and not wanted, run `python $PS ...` with Python 3.11 or later: the script needs only the standard library. Nothing else is installed.

## Checks

- **searched_and_failed_sources_reported**: the answer names which sources were searched and which failed or are off; a failed or empty source is not presented as absence of literature.
- **citations_from_returned_results**: every cited paper appears in a result or a fetch report of this session.
- **switched_off_sources_untouched**: no switched-off source was reached by any route, and no switch or read order changed without the user's instruction.

## Sources

- AI intent mapping: paper-search → research.literature-search (its search and its source switches) and research.paper-reading (its `fetch`).
- Source: open-paper-skills (pengqianhan/open-paper-skills@f85fd3dc, head) — `skills/paper-search/SKILL.md` and `scripts/paper_search.py`, packaged unchanged under `<package_root>/scripts/open-paper-skills/skills/paper-search/` (the skill file as `SKILL.source.md`). The script reimplements designs from alphaXiv OpenResearch (MIT) and google-deepmind science-skills (Apache-2.0), as its header states.
- Not packaged: `scripts/test_paper_search.py`.
- Changes for coexistence (ADR-0017):
  - The source's frontmatter triggers ("Use when ...") are not applied: they would trigger the original as a skill, and the coordinator classifies by meaning.
  - "Run from anywhere inside the repository" becomes the user's project (step 1): the packaged script lives under `<package_root>`, outside that project, and it finds the switch file from the working directory.
  - The source's `.env` template (`.env.example` in the author's repository) does not exist here: the `.env` is the user's project's, written by the user or by `keys --set NAME`.
  - The os-ui routes (switches from its **Papers** button, keys pasted under **Keys** in its Papers panel) are not followed: os-ui is the author's own interface and no supported host has it. Switches change through `sources`, keys through `.env` or `keys --set NAME`; the script's rate-limit message still names the panel, relay the `.env` route.
  - "other skills" in the off-on-every-route rule also covers the other capabilities of this package (step 2), which would otherwise be a second route to a switched-off source.
  - Installing `uv` when wanted, and `python $PS` when it is not, are this package's dependency rule (ADR-0007); the source names only `uv run`.
  - `--config <project>/memory/paper-sources.json` (step 7) is the script's own instruction, not in the skill text: the source's repository always has the switch file, a user's project may not.
- Runtime dependency: `uv` or Python 3.11+; optional `truststore`; optional user keys. The source gives `uv run` as the method.
- Hooks: the selected files define none.
- Harmonized by: prompts/harmonizer.md — its own role; `html-explanation` reads `literature_findings` when a search or a fetch was recorded before it. Since 2026-11-18 (owner decision) this capability and `html-explanation` are what the package takes from this source.

Strumenti richiesti

shell (richiesto)
Run the packaged TokenEconomizer command line with Python 3.10+. It reads and writes its own state under ~/.tokeneconomizer; apply and restore also edit the project's host settings file. The commands make no model call.

Hook e attivatori operativi

Evento: SessionStart
Azione: Inject the repository's learned facts as context, announce changed facts, newly left-out tools or a waiting proposal in one line, and fold earlier sessions whose end was not seen.
Politica: host-approved

  • shell
  • host-hooks

Evento: UserPromptSubmit
Azione: Open a prompt-turn for the failure-loop guard.
Politica: host-approved

  • shell
  • host-hooks

Evento: PostToolUse
Azione: Count the call in the turn's guard; deliver a redirect as context, then a one-line notice if the turn is still stuck. Never stops the turn. May start a detached judge job that calls a model through the user's own agent command line.
Politica: host-approved

  • shell
  • host-hooks

Evento: PostToolUseFailure
Azione: The same as PostToolUse, for a call that failed.
Politica: host-approved

  • shell
  • host-hooks

Evento: Stop
Azione: Close the turn; a turn that ended with passing checks feeds the repository's usual turn length.
Politica: host-approved

  • shell
  • host-hooks

Evento: SessionEnd
Azione: Hand the finished session to a detached fold job that updates facts, tool evidence and the cost ledger, and may later write a deny list to the project's host settings.
Politica: host-approved

  • shell
  • host-hooks

# Token Economy

Operates TokenEconomizer 0.1.0, which lowers the cost of coding-agent sessions in repositories the user works in often. It learns from finished sessions through three mechanisms: **micro-skills** (short repository facts stated at session start), **tool pruning** (unused tools left out through the host's own settings) and the **loop guard** (a redirect when a turn is stuck in repeated failures). `$TE` below is:

`python "<package_root>/scripts/tokeneconomizer/plugin/scripts/te_bootstrap.py" cli --cwd "<project root>"`

Add `--host codex`, `--host copilot` or `--host pi` on those hosts; the default is `claude`. When `python` is not Python 3.10 or newer, use the first that is among the interpreter named by `TE_PYTHON`, `python3` and `python`.

The full version is the packaged engine with `<package_root>/scripts/tokeneconomizer/plugin/README.md` and `<package_root>/scripts/tokeneconomizer/docs/PLUGIN.md`. Where this body differs, the packaged original wins, except for the changes listed in the Sources section. Open only what the task needs: in the README, `## Commands` for a command or argument not covered here, `## Settings` before changing a setting or explaining a value, `## What to expect` when the user asks when and how each mechanism acts, `## Repository map` for the opt-in `repomap` setting, `## Model calls and API keys` for a question about model calls or billing, `## Troubleshooting` when something fails. In PLUGIN.md, `## 1. What it does, hook by hook`, `## 4. State and privacy`, `## 5. Known limitations` and the paragraphs of `## 3. Verified agent behaviour` for the host in use, when the user wants more than the disclosure of step 4 or the host's version or behaviour departs from it.

## Behavior

1. **Report (read-only).** Run the matching command and show its output verbatim in a code block.
   - `$TE status`: what it learned and did here, and what the sessions cost. Add nothing, unless the output contains a warning: then explain the warning in one sentence.
   - `$TE microskills`: the facts it injects and those still forming. No commentary.
   - `$TE repos` (the same as `repos list`): every repository it keeps state for. If the list shows state recorded by an earlier version, say in one sentence that it is sorted out at the next session start, or now with `repos migrate`.
   - `$TE doctor`: checks Python, the state directory, the agents found, how this directory was identified, and the error log.
   - `$TE config show`: what is on, and every value in effect.
2. **Tool pruning.** `$TE toolprune show` is the default and shows the proposal. Pass `apply`, `restore` or `measure` (optionally with tool names) only when the user asked for that action; never add them yourself, and never run `apply` or `restore` unasked. `refresh-catalog` records the tools a session loads (Claude Code, Copilot). `apply` and `restore` edit the project's host settings (Claude Code: `.claude/settings.local.json`; Codex: `.codex/config.toml`; Copilot: `.github/copilot/settings.local.json`). On Claude Code `measure` makes two model calls through `claude -p`, and only when it is run. If the output is a proposal, end with one line saying how to apply it (ask this capability, which runs `$TE toolprune apply`) and that it takes effect from the next session.
3. **Settings and repository state.** `$TE config show` unless the user asked to change a setting; then `$TE config set KEY=VALUE ...` or `$TE config unset KEY ...`, with `--global` only if they asked for every repository. Never add `set` or `unset` yourself. If a setting was rejected, say why in one sentence. The three mechanisms are `microskills` (`on`, `off`, `envfacts`, `distiller`; off by default), `toolprune` (`on`/`auto`, `off`, `propose`) and `loopguard` (`on`/`nudge`, `off`); the other keys are in the README's `## Settings`. For state, `$TE repos list` unless the user asked for `migrate` or for `merge KEY [INTO]` (keys as the list shows them; INTO defaults to this repository); never run `migrate` or `merge` unasked. A merge keeps the old state directory under `~/.tokeneconomizer/merged/`.
   - On Codex, `config set`, `config unset`, `repos migrate`, `repos merge`, `toolprune apply` and `toolprune restore` write the engine's state under `~/.tokeneconomizer`, outside the workspace, which the sandbox keeps read-only: run that command with `sandbox_permissions` set to `"require_escalated"` and a one-line `justification`, so that Codex asks the user to approve it. `show`, `list` and `measure` need no approval.
4. **Automatic mode on** (only when the user asks to activate it). The mechanisms run only when the host calls the dispatcher on its hook events. This plugin never registers them by itself.
   - First say, in plain words, what activation does: the dispatcher runs at session start and end, on every prompt and on every tool call; state is kept in `~/.tokeneconomizer`; with the defaults tool pruning writes a deny list to the project's host settings after the repository's sessions have been idle for 60 minutes (`toolprune=propose` only proposes); the loop guard may call a judge model through the user's own agent command line (`claude -p` and the like), billed where their session is, sending digests (command templates, edited file basenames, error lines with paths and numbers masked, never file contents); micro-skills is off by default.
   - Say what this release was verified on by its authors: Claude Code 2.1.300 to 2.1.310, Codex 0.153.1 to 0.164.0, Copilot CLI 1.0.83 to 1.0.102, Pi 1.2.0 to 1.3.0, and that it lists Windows as a limitation. Compare with the host's actual version and name any gap.
   - After the user confirms, add the entries of `<package_root>/scripts/tokeneconomizer/plugin/hooks/hooks.json` (Codex: `codex-hooks.json`; Copilot: `copilot-hooks.json`, in the same folder) to the project's host settings: six events, five in the Codex manifest, which has no `PostToolUseFailure`. Keep each entry's timeout and the arguments the manifest puts after the launcher (`--host codex`, `--host copilot`), and replace the launcher itself with `python "<package_root>/scripts/tokeneconomizer/plugin/scripts/te_bootstrap.py" hook`, with `<package_root>` written out as the absolute path. On Claude Code the file is `.claude/settings.local.json`. Merge into what is there; refuse to write a file that does not parse. Tell the user it takes effect from the next session.
5. **Automatic mode off.** Remove exactly the entries that point at this plugin's `te_bootstrap.py`, nothing else. The learned state stays in `~/.tokeneconomizer` until someone deletes it; deleting it is the user's call. For one session only, `TE_DISABLE=1` in the environment turns the whole engine off.

## Output handoff

Resolve `<package_root>` with the `package_root` returned beside these instructions, never against the consumer project. Return `economy_report` (the command run and its output, or what was explained) and `economy_changes` (each setting, deny rule, hook entry or state move that changed, with the file, or `none`) as JSON strings. For a mapped step, submit them through the coordinator's `record` command with the step's `map_id` and `capability`. Do not edit `<state_dir>/map.md` or `<state_dir>/state.json`; the coordinator is their only writer.

## Specifics

- Without the automatic mode the commands work but have nothing new to show: the engine learns from a session once it ends, through its hooks.
- If the original TokenEconomizer plugin is also installed in the host, its hooks and these would both run. One of the two must be off.
- The hook entries hold an absolute path to this plugin's folder. After this plugin is updated or moved, run activation again so the path is current; a stale path makes the hook fail and the session carries on.
- Every hook fails open: any error becomes an empty output (no change) and a traceback in `~/.tokeneconomizer/errors.log`. When the hooks seem to do nothing, run `$TE doctor` and read its errors.log lines.
- The deny-list writer adds and removes only deny rules it recorded adding, never one the user wrote. `toolprune restore` gives back what the engine removed, and only that; what is given back is never removed again, unless `toolprune apply NAME` removes it again.
- A learned fact is text injected into the agent's context, derived from the sessions' command output, which a repository controls. On a repository the user does not trust, use `microskills=envfacts`, or read what it learned with `$TE microskills`.
- Runtime dependency: Python 3.10 or newer, already required to run this coordinator. Nothing is installed.

## Checks

- **output_shown_verbatim**: the command's output is shown as it was printed, with the command that produced it.
- **no_change_without_explicit_request**: no `apply`, `restore`, `set`, `unset`, `migrate`, `merge` or hook edit ran unless the user asked for that action in this task.
- **activation_effects_disclosed_before_registering**: before any hook entry was written, the user was told about the hook events, the state folder, the automatic deny list, the judge's model calls and the verified host versions, and confirmed.
- **hooks_registered_or_removed_exactly**: the settings file parses after the edit and contains exactly the entries of the host's manifest (six; five on Codex) pointing at this plugin's dispatcher (activation) or none of them (deactivation), with every other entry unchanged; when nothing was registered or removed, record this as not applicable.

## Sources

- AI intent mapping: the upstream commands `status`, `microskills`, `repos`, `doctor`, `config show` → cost.economy-report; `toolprune` → cost.tool-pruning; `config set/unset`, `repos migrate/merge` and the hook manifests → cost.economy-settings. The earlier command names `facts` and `untool` are not exposed.
- Source: tokeneconomizer (microsoft/TokenEconomizer@ec8ff5ec, release v0.1.0) — the `tokeneconomizer/**` package, `plugin/scripts/te_bootstrap.py`, `plugin/hooks/*.json`, `plugin/README.md` and `docs/PLUGIN.md`, packaged unchanged under `<package_root>/scripts/tokeneconomizer/`. Read at intake and carried in steps 1 to 4, not packaged: `plugin/slash-commands/*.md`, `plugin/codex-skills/*/SKILL.md` and the supported-versions table of the root `README.md`.
- Changes for coexistence (ADR-0017):
  - The source registers its hooks when its plugin is installed; here they are registered only on the user's request, after the disclosure of step 4. This is the package's delivery decision (`delivery.json`): default activation would compete with the host's and the coordinator's hook wiring and has not been run live from this release.
  - The README's install and approval steps (`## Before you start`, `## Claude Code`, `## Codex`, `## Copilot CLI`, `## Pi`) are not followed: they install the original plugin beside this one, whose hooks would then run twice, and a capability never installs the source plugin itself.
  - Commands run as `$TE ...`, not as `/tokeneconomizer:<command>`, `$tokeneconomizer:<command>`, `/te <command>` or `~/.tokeneconomizer/bin/te`: the source's slash commands, Codex skills and Pi extension are not registered, since they would trigger the original beside the coordinator, which classifies by meaning.
  - The POSIX launchers `te` and `te-hook` give way to a direct call of `te_bootstrap.py` (`cli` or `hook`): the plugin-root variables of the hook manifests would point at this plugin's root, where no `scripts/te-hook` exists. Lost with the launcher: its `{}` answer when no Python is on `PATH` (the host then reports the hook command as failed) and the Codex skills' advice to start a new session when the launcher is missing.
  - The source shows command output to the user only; here it is also returned through the coordinator, the single owner of recorded outputs.
- Hooks: passive catalog entries with policy `host-approved`: nothing registers them at build, install or classification time. The Pi extension (`plugin/pi/tokeneconomizer.ts`) is not adopted.
- Not adopted: the upstream plugin manifests and marketplace file, the slash commands and Codex skills as files (their instructions are steps 1 to 3), the POSIX `te` and `te-hook` launchers (the Python bootstrap is called directly, which also runs on Windows), `experiments/**`, `tests/**`, `scripts/**`, `docs/assets/**`.
- Runtime dependency: Python 3.10+. Optional, off by default and not installed here: `aider-chat` for the repository map.
- Harmonized by: prompts/harmonizer.md — its own role; no other capability controls session cost. It shares no output and no settings file with them: its deny rules live in the host's settings, and its state outside the project.

# Engineering Review

Produces a report the user asked for, given in full, and changes no code. Order of importance: correct, safe, holds under load, tested, fast, lean.

The packaged original of the requested intent is the full version and wins where this body differs, except for the changes listed in the Sources section: `<package_root>/scripts/ponytail/skills/ponytail-review/SKILL.source.md` for a change review, `<package_root>/scripts/ponytail/skills/ponytail-audit/SKILL.source.md` for a repository or folder audit. Open the section a step names when you reach it.

## Behavior

1. **Scope.** Change review: what the user names (uncommitted or staged changes, a branch, a PR link, files); nothing named: the uncommitted changes, or the last commit if there are none. Audit: the folder, package or whole repo the user names; nothing named: the whole repo.
2. **Read before judging.**
   - Review: the diff, then the code it touches: callers of every changed function, the functions it calls, the tests, the README. Trace the real flow (where data comes in, what is stored, what goes out). When a signature, return value or behavior changes, grep every caller.
   - Audit: the README, deploy and build config, dependency list, entry points and tests. Trace the main flows end to end and read those paths fully: user input, money, auth, data writes, background jobs, anything shared between processes. In a big repo go deep where a mistake costs the most, not file by file, and say which parts you did not read.
   - Both: find the expected load (one person running a script, or many users and processes at once), judge scale against it and say which load you assumed.
3. **Look for** six classes, in this order: Bug, Risk, Scale, Missing test, Speed, Lean. Open `## 2. Look for` of the intent's file for what each covers; the lists differ between review and audit. Missing test means one good test that fails when risky logic breaks, not coverage. Big slowdowns are problems, small speed wins are suggestions. Lean is delete, reuse, stdlib / native, yagni, merge, split; split by job, never by line count and never into helpers that only make a function shorter.
4. **Check before you report.** Every finding needs a concrete case (this input or situation leads to this wrong result): no case, no finding. Review: re-read the lines and confirm the caller exists, the value can really be empty, the code really is unused. Audit: before calling code unused, grep the whole tree, including tests, fixtures, config and string or dynamic references. A shortcut marked with a `shortcut:` (or older `ponytail:`) comment that names its limit is a decision, not a finding, unless the expected load already crosses it. No style taste, no "consider", no vague worries.
5. **Fixes.** Propose the smallest fix that works and prefer fixes that delete code. Never add layers, frameworks or config the problem does not need.
6. **Write the report** in very simple English: short sentences, everyday words, a technical term explained at first use; the reader may never have seen this code.
   - Start with `What this change does:` in two or three sentences; an audit starts with `What this repo does:` and adds the load assumed.
   - Three groups, empty ones skipped (audit: most important first). **Must fix:** bug, security, data loss, breaks at the expected load. **Should fix:** risky code without a test, real slowness, duplication, a function that mixes jobs, code that should not exist. **Nice to have:** small speed-ups, shorter forms.
   - Number findings across all groups. Each has a bold title with its location (`path/file.py:L40-52`) and all four parts, one or two short sentences each: **What this is:**, **Problem:**, **Fix:**, **If we skip it:**. The worked example is in `## 4. Output` of either file.
   - Audit only: at most 20 findings; if smaller ones were left out, say how many.
7. **End.**
   - Review: `Verdict: Ship.` or `Verdict: fix 1 and 3 first.`; `Lean: -<N> lines possible.` when lean findings exist; `Not checked:` one line, if something mattered and you could not check it. Nothing found: `What this change does:`, then `Looks good. Ship.` and one line on what you checked.
   - Audit: `Verdict:` one line, healthy or what to fix first; `Lean: -<N> lines, -<M> dependencies possible.` when lean findings exist; `Not checked:` the parts you did not read or could not run. Nothing found: `What this repo does:`, then `Healthy. Nothing to fix.` and one line on what you checked.

## Output handoff

Return `code_review_findings` (numbered findings and verdict) and `code_review_coverage` (scope, assumed load, evidence checked, checks run and uninspected areas) as JSON strings. For a mapped step, submit them through the coordinator's `record` command with the step's `map_id` and `capability`. Do not edit `<state_dir>/map.md` or `<state_dir>/state.json`; the coordinator is their only writer.

## Specifics

- Work-map's per-slice acceptance review remains part of implementation; this report is a separate step only when it is requested. Design-review keeps design-system, accessibility and visual ownership; this capability owns software-behavior findings.
- Apply fixes only when the user also requests implementation, through the authorized implementation step.
- Git, search and test tools are assessed case by case; the source prescribes no installation procedure. There is no adopted hook or background work.

## Checks

- **target_and_load_stated**: the selected scope and expected-load assumption are explicit.
- **connected_flows_inspected**: relevant callers and end-to-end flows were read or recorded as gaps.
- **findings_have_concrete_evidence**: every finding has a concrete case, re-read and confirmed lines, the smallest fix that works and all four parts.
- **limits_respected**: documented shortcuts and the requested scope were respected; an audit shows at most 20 findings and says how many smaller ones were left out.
- **report_only**: source code was not changed.

## Sources

- Source: ponytail (DietrichGebert/ponytail@7801d061243d7b753bad0e0b3c057cd250b11755, release v5.3.3, MIT) — `skills/ponytail-review/SKILL.md` and `skills/ponytail-audit/SKILL.md`, packaged as `<package_root>/scripts/ponytail/skills/ponytail-review/SKILL.source.md` and `<package_root>/scripts/ponytail/skills/ponytail-audit/SKILL.source.md`.
- AI mapping: ponytail-review → engineering.change-review; ponytail-audit → engineering.codebase-audit. One report responsibility preserves two scopes; source names alone did not decide the merge. Outputs are separate from design-review's findings/fixes and TokenEconomizer's measured reports.
- Changes for coexistence (ADR-0017):
  - The trigger phrases, `/ponytail-review` and `/ponytail-audit` are not carried: the coordinator classifies by meaning.
  - The numbering "so the user can say "fix 2 and 5"" is kept, but a fix request is a separate implementation step (one capability per step).
  - The report is also handed over as `code_review_findings` and `code_review_coverage` through the coordinator (output handoff); its wording and format stay the source's.
- Original lifecycle hooks, native UI modules and mode state are outside this curated selection; `hooks: []` does not claim the upstream has no hooks. Slash routing and plugin installation were not adopted.

Harmonized by: `prompts/harmonizer.md` (2026-11-12). Compared with the pinned originals under ADR-0017; second pass the same day: an entry prompt in the package's words with pointers to the packaged originals.
